newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle blasts off on research mission.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle blasts off on research mission.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery soared into orbit on Thursday with six astronauts and a multitude of scientific experiments aboard.
The $2-billion winged space ship surged off its launch pad at the Kennedy Space Centre into a hazy summer sky at 10:41 a.m. EDT (1441 GMT) after a trouble-free countdown.
Aboard the shuttle were mission commander Curt Brown, co-pilot Kent Rominger, mission specialists Jan Davis, Robert Curbeam and Stephen Robinson and Canadian researcher Bjarni Tryggvason.
Minutes before the launch, controllers wished Rominger a happy birthday. The shuttle's co-pilot turned 41 on Thursday.
"We're about to light your candles," orbiter test director Roger Gillette said.
"Thanks for that birthday wish," Rominger replied from the cockpit. "They'll be the two best candles I've ever had."

The rain showers and thick clouds that forecasters had feared might delay the shuttle's launch never materialised, but hazy conditions and patchy cloud obscured most of the shuttle's thundering climb to orbit.

Seven hours after launch, the astronauts were to use the shuttle's robot arm to deploy a German-built free-flying satellite that will monitor the Earth's protective ozone layer. The 7,000-lb (3,200-kg) spacecraft will fly free of the shuttle for nine days before the astronauts return to pick it up.

During the 11-day mission, the crew will also point a telescope at Comet Hale-Bopp, test a Japanese robot arm intended for use on the planned international space station, and grow colon cancer cells for medical research.
Tryggvason, a Canadian scientist who was born in Reykjavik, Iceland, is flying aboard the shuttle to test a device designed to isolate delicate experiments from vibrations on the space station.
The president of Iceland, Olafur Ragnar Grimsson, watched the launch from a VIP viewing site four miles (6.5 km) from the pad.
"Splendid. The noise and vibrations were an unforgettable experience," he said. "We are a nation of discoverers and settlers and we consider this a continuation of a great Viking tradition."
Shuttle skipper Curt Brown told a recent news conference the mission is "just jam packed full of activities. We have about everything."
The astronauts plan to accomplish about 40 scientific objectives before returning to earth at the Florida spaceport on Aug. 18.
